propositions.text: This is an appeal of an April 23, 2021 RPD decision denying the Appellant's refugee claim under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: This is an appeal of an April 23, 2021 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Board) denying the Appellant's claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is an appeal of the April 23, 2021 RPD decision denying the Appellant's refugee claim under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: The Appellant fears persecution from the Turkish government due to his support of the HDP and his Kurdish status within the HDP.
propositions.quote: The Appellant, a Turkish national, claims that he fears persecution from the Turkish government due to i) his support of the Peoples' Democratic Party of Turkey (HDP) and ii) his status as a Kurdish member of the HDP.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims fear of persecution from Turkey due to his HDP support and Kurdish membership in the HDP.

propositions.text: The appeal is denied for the reasons that follow.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I deny this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court denies the appeal for reasons that follow.

propositions.text: The Appellant is a long-standing HDP supporter with various activities including visits, rallies, financial contributions, and membership since 2018.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is a long-standing supporter of the HDP. His involvement with the Party was as follows: from time to time he visited the local HDP office; he attended election rallies; he contributed financially to the HDP; in 2015, he XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the Party; in XXXX 2018, he joined the HDP; during the June 2018 general elections, he again XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the Party and worked at an XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant is a long-standing HDP supporter with various activities including visits, rallies, financial contributions, and membership since 2018.

propositions.text: After 2018 election, gendarmes warned the Appellant to stop supporting HDP or face false accusations and extorted money multiple times.
propositions.quote: Shortly after the 2018 election, officers from a special operations unit ("gendarmes") advised the Appellant that they knew he was a member and supporter of the HDP. They warned him that if he did not stop supporting the Party, they would accuse him of selling illegal XXXX from the XXXX XXXX he owned with his father and brother. The gendarmes extorted money from him twice and regular police officers did so about ten times.

propositions.text: In 2019, the Appellant closed his business due to extortion.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2019, he closed the XXXX XXXX because of the extortion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that after 2018 election, gendarmes warned and extorted the Appellant, who closed his business in 2019 due to extortion.

propositions.text: In 2019, gendarmes raided the Appellant's home, detained him, threatened torture if he continued HDP activities, prompting him to leave Turkey.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, 2019, the gendarmes raided his home. They detained him for XXXX days and warned him that no matter where he went, they would find him and "get" him. When he was released, he was told not to engage in HDP activities or else he would be tortured. As a result, he decided to leave Turkey.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that in 2019, gendarmes raided, detained, threatened the Appellant, leading him to leave Turkey.

propositions.text: The Appellant came to Canada in 2019 on a visitor visa, delayed asylum claim to protect family visits, family joined later, and he filed his claim in July 2019.
propositions.quote: He came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019, travelling on a visitor visa he had obtained in 2016 in connection with a visit to his cousin who lives in Canada. He did not claim asylum upon arrival because he did not want to jeopardize his family's ability to visit him in Canada. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, his wife and two children joined him in Canada. On July 26, 2019, XXXX days after his family's return to Turkey, he signed his Basis of Claim form.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant came to Canada in 2019 on visitor visa, delayed asylum claim, family joined later, and he filed claim in July 2019.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks admission of new evidence: letters from father and brother and a family property title deed.
propositions.quote: The Appellant seeks the admission of the following at appeal: 1) a XXXX XXXX, 2021 letter from his father confirming many of the facts relating to his claim and discussing the dismissal of Kurds from their jobs in Turkey; 2) a XXXX XXXX, 2021 letter from his brother confirming many of the facts relating to his claim and stating that, in Turkey, the police, the gendarmerie, the security forces, and the mafia are intertwined; and 3) a title deed to the family XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant seeks admission of new evidence: letters from father and brother and a family property title deed.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence at RAD appeal to evidence arising after RPD rejection, not reasonably available then, or not reasonably expected to be presented then.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA limits the admission of new evidence in an appeal before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to evidence that: 1) arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim; 2) was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim; or 3) an appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

propositions.text: Singh and Raza require new evidence at appeal to meet newness, credibility, and relevance criteria.
propositions.quote: the Federal Court of Appeal held in the Singh case1-relying on its previous decision in Raza2-that the following factors must be met before new evidence could be admitted under subsection 110(4): newness, credibility, and relevance.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence at RAD appeal to evidence meeting newness, credibility, and relevance criteria per Singh and Raza.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues RAD must consider severe consequences of not admitting evidence, citing Asri case and Justice Russell's reasoning.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that there is yet another factor that I must consider in assessing the admissibility of the evidence he seeks to adduce at appeal. He relies on the Asri case,4 where Mr. Justice Russell held that while the RAD did not have to accept Mr. Arsi's explanation as to why the new evidence he attempted to adduce at appeal was not reasonably available before the rejection of the claim, if it did not, it may be obliged to consider "the severe consequences of not admitting [the] documentation."

propositions.text: Justice Russell held RAD may need to consider conscience of Canadians to avoid refusing genuine claims when evidence is likely conclusive support.
propositions.quote: Mr. Justice Russell held that the RAD may be required, as part of its deliberations on admissibility, to ensure that was not refusing a genuine claim, thereby shocking the conscience of Canadians: The documentation was not disregarded as either irrelevant or because it was not genuine. Accordingly, there was a distinct possibility that the RAD was refusing a genuine claim because the Applicant had failed to convince it that these documents were not reasonably available earlier. In my view, this would shock the conscience of Canadians, who would expect the RAD to consider this possibility as a part of its deliberations on admissibility and, given what was at stake, consider some way of avoiding possible tragic consequence that did not require a disregard of the governing statutory provisions and the overall purpose of the IRPA which includes, inter alia, the protection of genuine refugees.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RAD must consider severe consequences of not admitting evidence, citing Justice Russell's Asri case reasoning about conscience of Canadians.

propositions.text: Justice Russell's additional requirement to consider conscience is limited to cases where evidence likely conclusively supports the claim, not broadly applicable.
propositions.quote: I find that the additional requirement that the RAD would consider the conscience of Canadians-and "seek out" a way to consider the possibility that it might be refusing a genuine claim-as part of its deliberations on the admissibility of new evidence at appeal is limited to the circumstances of the Asri case, i.e., where the evidence the applicant sought the admission of was "likely conclusive support of the Applicant's refugee claim."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Justice Russell's conscience consideration is limited to cases with likely conclusive evidence, not broadly applicable.

propositions.text: If Justice Russell intended a broad requirement, he would have said so; such would conflict with Singh and Raza's clear tests on new evidence.
propositions.quote: Had Mr. Justice Russell intended to impose this additional requirement in all cases, he would have made this explicit. After all, such a requirement would be tantamount a reassessment of the findings in Singh and Raza, where the Federal Court of Appeal so carefully considered the issue of new evidence at appeal and, with Singh, the meaning of subsection 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Justice Russell did not intend a broad new evidence admission requirement, which would conflict with Singh and Raza.

propositions.text: RAD cannot ignore subsection 110(4) conditions; Singh holds these conditions are inescapable and leave no discretion to RAD.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal in Singh clearly ruled that the RAD was not vested with the discretion to disregard the conditions set out in subsection 110(4). It described the conditions of subsection 110(4), as "inescapable" and leaving "no room for discretion on the part of the RAD."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Singh holds RAD has no discretion to disregard subsection 110(4) conditions for new evidence admission.

propositions.text: Singh rejected a flexible interpretation of subsection 110(4) despite arguments about limited timeframes and access to full fact-based appeal.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal in Singh considered and rejected Madam Justice Gagné's (now Associate Chief Justice Gagné) reasoning in the Singh case at the Federal Court level, where she called for a flexible interpretation of subsection 110(4). It referred to her reasoning that a strict interpretation of subsection 110(4) would unfairly limit an applicant's access to a full fact-based appeal and that "the reduced timeframes within which claimants must submit their documents...support the flexible interpretation of the admissibility criteria." However, it concluded that these considerations did "not suffice to set aside the clear legislative intention to not authorize any new evidence on appeal other than in very specific and carefully defined circumstances."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Singh rejected flexible interpretation of subsection 110(4) despite arguments about timeframes and access to full appeal.

propositions.text: A broad flexible approach to subsection 110(4) would ignore Parliament's clear tests and Singh/Raza analysis.
propositions.quote: Such an approach would surely be ignoring the clear tests set out by the Parliament of Canada in subsection 110(4) and elaborated upon by the Federal Court of Appeal in its Singh/Raza analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a broad flexible approach to subsection 110(4) would ignore Parliament's clear tests and Singh/Raza analysis.

propositions.text: Justice Russell's conscience consideration is limited to cases with likely conclusive evidence; Appellant's evidence does not meet this.
propositions.quote: Instead, I find that Mr. Justice Russell intended to limit his finding to the circumstances of the Asri claim, i.e., where a finding that certain evidence the applicant sought the admission of at appeal was likely to provide conclusive support of the Applicant's refugee claim. In the instant case, the evidence the Appellant seeks the admission of does not meet this requirement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Justice Russell's conscience consideration limited to likely conclusive evidence cases; Appellant's evidence does not qualify.

propositions.text: Letters from father and brother do not meet subsection 110(4) first requirement as they restate prior facts and do not arise after claim rejection.
propositions.quote: The information provided in the letters did not arise after the rejection of the claim; instead the information represents a restatement of the story the Appellant gave to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds letters from family do not meet subsection 110(4) first requirement as they restate prior facts, not new events.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues he was unaware of need for family supporting evidence and that his limited education and counsel representation justify flexible application of subsection 110(4).
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he was not aware that he needed to provide supporting evidence from his family members...given his limited education, his lack of awareness was reasonable...he relies on the Federal Court of Appeal's observation in Singh...that the RAD "always has the freedom to apply the condition of subsection 110(4) with more or less flexibility depending on the circumstances of the case."

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues he was unaware of need for family evidence and urges flexible subsection 110(4) application due to limited education and counsel.

propositions.text: RAD appeal is paper-based and not a second chance to complete deficient record; applicants must put best foot forward to RPD.
propositions.quote: An analysis of the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD begins with the premise that the appeal of an RPD decision is intended to be a paper-based appeal...A RAD appeal is not a second chance to submit evidence to answer weaknesses identified by the RPD...An applicant is required to put his or her best foot forward to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD appeal is paper-based, not a second chance to complete record; applicants must put best foot forward to RPD.

propositions.text: Given counsel representation, Appellant should have known importance of supporting evidence about HDP link; education is of little relevance.
propositions.quote: In view of the jurisprudence and, given that the Appellant was represented by experienced counsel, I find that he would have (or should have) known of the importance of providing supporting evidence about his link to the Party-the issue at the very heart of this claim. The extent of his education is of little relevance.

propositions.text: Appellant's single letter from HDP Provincial President is short, impersonal, and inconsistent with his testimony, failing to mention some claimed activities.
propositions.quote: While it is true that he did provide a single document meant to show his link to the Party, his counsel would (or should) have been aware of the risk of operating on the assumption that a single piece of evidence was all that was required. This is especially so in view of the content of the letter. As discussed in my analysis below, the XXXX XXXX, 2020 letter is short, impersonal, and attributes activities to the Appellant that do not correspond with his testimony, while failing to mention activities that he claims to have performed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant should have known importance of supporting evidence given counsel; his single letter is short, impersonal, and inconsistent with testimony.

propositions.text: This is not a case where the appellant or counsel should have been surprised by the level of proof demanded by the RPD decision-maker.
propositions.quote: While there may be instances where a represented claimant may be justifiably surprised by the level of proof demanded by an RPD decision-maker,17 this is not such a case.

propositions.text: The appellant's evidence was not so persuasive as to make it unreasonable to expect additional evidence at the RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: It is not a case where the evidence provided by the Appellant was so very persuasive that it would be unreasonable to have expected the Appellant (or his counsel) to have adduced additional evidence at his RPD hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant should not have been surprised by the proof level and his evidence was not so persuasive to excuse additional evidence.

propositions.text: The two letters do not meet subsection 110(4) requirements and are inadmissible.
propositions.quote: The two letters do not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4). As such, I need not consider whether they comply with the factors outlined in Singh. They are inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the two letters inadmissible for failing subsection 110(4) requirements.

propositions.text: The appellant argues he could not reasonably have been expected to provide the title document because he did not think it was needed, citing limited education and a letter from the HDP.
propositions.quote: Once again, the Appellant argues that he could not reasonably have been expected to have provided the title document showing that his family owns a XXXX XXXX because he did not think he needed to. Once again, he points to his limited education and the fact that he submitted a letter from the HDP.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues he was not reasonably expected to provide the title document due to limited education and reliance on an HDP letter.

propositions.text: The appellant's claim of ignorance about proving ownership is unreasonable given his representation and the interconnectedness of ownership with his claim.
propositions.quote: For the reasons discussed above-including that he is ably represented-his claim that he did not know about the need to prove ownership of the XXXX is not reasonable.

propositions.text: His co-ownership of the XXXX is linked to alleged threats, extortion, and raids, undermining his claim of ignorance.
propositions.quote: After all, his co-ownership of the XXXX XXXX is interconnected with his overall claim: it was linked to the alleged threats from the gendarmes...

propositions.text: Providing supporting evidence about his link to the HDP undermines his claim of ignorance about needing ownership evidence.
propositions.quote: That he provided supporting evidence about his link to the HDP does nothing support his claim that he did not know that he needed to provide evidence that his family owned a XXXX XXXX; to the contrary, it undermines that claim by showing that he was indeed aware of the importance of providing supporting evidence in a refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's ignorance claim unreasonable and undermined by his evidence and claim context.

propositions.text: The title document does not meet subsection 110(4) requirements and is inadmissible.
propositions.quote: The title document does not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) and, as such, is inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the title document inadmissible for failing subsection 110(4) requirements.

propositions.text: The request for a hearing under subsection 110(6) is denied because no new evidence was admitted.
propositions.quote: Because no new evidence has been admitted, the request for a hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA must be denied.

paragraphs.summary: The court denies the hearing request due to no new evidence admitted.

propositions.text: The determinative issue in this case is credibility.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this case is credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies credibility as the determinative issue.

propositions.text: The standard of review of the RPD's decision is correctness because the RPD had no meaningful advantage in findings.
propositions.quote: In my review of the RPD's decision, I will apply a standard of correctness.19 This is not a case where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in making its findings.20

paragraphs.summary: The court will apply correctness standard as the RPD had no meaningful advantage in findings.

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant lacked credibility, was not a long-standing HDP supporter, and was not at risk due to party involvement.
propositions.quote: The RPD held 1) based on problems with his credibility, including the provision of inadequate supporting evidence, that the Appellant was not a long-standing supporter of the Party...

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant's HDP membership and Kurdish ethnicity did not place him at risk.
propositions.quote: In addition, it held 2) that, while he was a member of the HDP as of XXXX 2020, that membership, in conjunction with his Kurdish ethnicity, did not place him at risk.

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant's Kurdish status alone would not lead to persecution or harm.
propositions.quote: Finally, it held 3) that his status as a Kurd would not lead to a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of other harm.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant lacked credibility, was not at risk due to HDP involvement or Kurdish status alone.

propositions.text: The appellant contests the RPD's findings on risk from HDP involvement and Kurdish HDP membership but not from Kurdish ethnicity alone.
propositions.quote: The Appellant contests the RPD's findings that he was not at risk because 1) of his involvement with the HDP or 2) of his status as a Kurdish member of the HDP. However, he does not contest its finding 3) that his Kurdish ethnicity alone would not lead to a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of other harm.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant contests risk findings related to HDP involvement but not Kurdish ethnicity alone.

propositions.text: The court agrees with the uncontested RPD finding that Kurdish ethnicity alone does not pose serious risk and will not discuss it further.
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the RPD's uncontested finding that he does not face a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of other harm in Turkey due to his Kurdish ethnicity alone and I agree with it. As it is uncontested, I will not discuss it further.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the uncontested RPD finding that Kurdish ethnicity alone does not pose serious risk.

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellant's knowledge of the HDP was insufficient for his claimed long-term involvement.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that the Appellant's knowledge of the HDP was not commensurate with his claimed long-term involvement with the Party.

propositions.text: The appellant's testimony on HDP policies was vague and brief, lacking detail on policies and platforms.
propositions.quote: He lacked the ability to speak about the HDP's policies and his testimony on the subject was vague and brief.

propositions.text: The RPD did not find the appellant's lack of knowledge explained by his incomplete high school education.
propositions.quote: It considered that the Appellant had not completed high school; however, it did not find that this explained his lack of knowledge.

propositions.text: The RPD expected detailed testimony about HDP's socialist, secular, democratic, women's and minorities' rights, anti-capitalist, and pro-worker policies.
propositions.quote: It held that he should have been able to provide detailed testimony, without prompting, about the HDP, including that it is a socialist and secular party which advocates for democracy, women's and minorities' rights, and is anti-capitalist and pro-worker.

propositions.text: The appellant had some knowledge of the party's leaders and formation year but overall knowledge was deficient.
propositions.quote: While it acknowledged that the Appellant did have some knowledge of the Party (he knew the names of the two current leaders of the Party and the year it was formed), it nevertheless found his knowledge deficient.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant's knowledge of the HDP insufficient and his testimony vague despite some basic knowledge.

propositions.text: The appellant argues the RPD's expectations were too high for a rank-and-file supporter with limited education.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD's expectations were too high; his answers were consistent with what could reasonably be expected of a "rank-and-file supporter" with a limited education.

propositions.text: He argues his loyalty is explained by family support of pro-Kurdish parties and Kurdish loyalty to the Party.
propositions.quote: His loyalty to the Party may reasonably be explained by his family's long-term support of pro-Kurdish parties for decades, and/or the loyalty a Kurd might reasonably have to a Party devoted to Kurdish people's freedom.

propositions.text: He argues the RPD failed to give adequate weight to his knowledge of party leaders and formation year.
propositions.quote: He also argues that the RPD failed to give his knowledge of the Party (as noted, he knew the names of the two current leaders of the Party and the year it was formed) adequate weight in reaching its finding.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD's expectations were too high and failed to properly weigh his knowledge and loyalty explanations.

propositions.text: The appellant argues the RPD acted unfairly by faulting him for not knowing economic views he was not questioned about.
propositions.quote: In addition, he argues that the RPD acted unfairly because it faulted him for i) not knowing about the Party's views on economic matters, when he was not even questioned about them

propositions.text: He argues it was unfair to fault him for not stating the HDP was anti-capitalist based on an undisclosed Wikipedia article source.
propositions.quote: and ii) not stating that the HDP was anti-capitalist, when its source for its statement that it was anti-capitalise was an article that was a) not disclosed to the Appellant and b) from Wikipedia, an unreliable source.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD acted unfairly by faulting him for knowledge he was not questioned on and for reliance on undisclosed Wikipedia source.

propositions.text: The appellant's claim of deep involvement conflicts with his claim of being a mere rank-and-file supporter with limited knowledge.
propositions.quote: There is a certain tension in this claim. On the one hand, the Appellant's claim is based on him having been so involved with the HDP that the Turkish authorities came to know of his support and want to harm him because of it. At the same time, in view of his superficial testimony about the Party, he now argues that he is a mere "rank and file" supporter of the HDP...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds tension between the appellant's claimed deep involvement and limited knowledge of the HDP.

propositions.text: The appellant's testimony about HDP policies was very shallow and insufficient for claimed involvement level.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's testimony about why he supports the Party and what he believes it stands for was very shallow indeed.

propositions.text: It is unlikely the Party would entrust public representation to someone with such limited knowledge as the appellant claims.
propositions.quote: It is highly unlikely that the Party would entrust someone to publicly represent it-by working at an XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX-if that person was so lacking in knowledge that they were unable to provide even the most basic details about party policy...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's shallow testimony unlikely for someone entrusted with public representation by the HDP.

propositions.text: The appellant's limited knowledge conflicts with his claim he would continue pro-Kurdish political involvement risking his life.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Appellant's limited knowledge of the Party is incompatible with his claim that, if he returned to Turkey, he would "continue to involve [him]self in pro-Kurdish politics...

propositions.text: It is highly unlikely someone willing to risk so much for pro-Kurdish politics would know so little about the cause.
propositions.quote: I find that it is highly unlikely that someone who feels so strongly about pro-Kurdish politics that he would be willing to risk his life...would know so little about the cause he is willing to risk so much to champion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's limited knowledge incompatible with his claimed strong commitment to pro-Kurdish politics.

propositions.text: The RPD's failure to ask about economic policies was not unfair as the appellant could have spoken about them unprompted.
propositions.quote: As to the Appellant's first fairness argument, while it is true that the RPD did not ask him about the HHDP's economic policies, I can see no reason why fairness would have required that it did so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no unfairness in the RPD not asking about economic policies as the appellant could have volunteered them.

propositions.text: The RPD may take notice of specialized knowledge but must notify parties and allow representations before relying on it.
propositions.quote: The law on the use of specialized knowledge by an RPD decision-maker is set out at paragraph 170(i) of the IRPA...

propositions.text: Rule 22 requires notice and opportunity to respond before using specialized knowledge in RPD hearings.
propositions.quote: Rule 22 of the RPD Rules23 limits the RPD's reliance on specialized knowledge: Before using any information or opinion that is within its specialized knowledge, the Division must notify the claimant or protected person and...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RPD's legal duty to notify and allow response before using specialized knowledge evidence.

propositions.text: RPD's reliance on evidence not before the appellant breaches procedural fairness as established in N'Sungani and Kirichenko cases.
propositions.quote: The RPD's reliance on evidence that was not before the Appellant means that there has, ipso facto, been a breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD breached procedural fairness by relying on evidence not disclosed to the appellant.

propositions.text: What is the appropriate remedy for the RPD's breach of natural justice?
propositions.quote: The question then becomes what the appropriate remedy is for the RPD's breach of natural justice.

propositions.text: Breach of procedural fairness usually voids the hearing and decision, but an exception exists for 'special circumstances' where outcome is inevitable or claim hopeless.
propositions.quote: Ordinarily, a breach of procedural fairness voids the hearing and the resulting decision but an exception to this rule exists...This exception stems from Mobil Oil Canada Ltd. v. Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board...where the Supreme Court of Canada explained that a breach of procedural fairness does not require a new hearing in "special circumstances" where the claim in question is otherwise "hopeless" or the outcome reached was "inevitable".

propositions.text: In Mir, procedural error did not require setting aside decision because chance to respond would not have impacted final decision.
propositions.quote: In Mir, Mr. Justice Kelen made clear that the procedural error in that case did not, in the circumstances, necessitate setting the decision aside because, even if the applicant had had the chance to respond, it would not have impacted the final decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court asks what remedy fits the RPD's breach of natural justice, citing case law that procedural fairness breaches usually void decisions except in special circumstances where outcome is inevitable.

propositions.text: Found procedural error by RPD relying on specialized knowledge violating Rule 22 but will not consider Wikipedia in reassessment.
propositions.quote: While I have found a breach of procedural fairness arising from the RPD's reliance on its specialized knowledge in contravention of Rule 22, I will not have regard to the Wikipedia article in my reassessment of the Appellant's credibility.

propositions.text: RPD's error will not impact reassessment; no need to set RPD decision aside.
propositions.quote: As such, the RPD's error will have no impact on my reassessment and there is no need to set the RPD's decision aside.

propositions.text: No need to decide if Wikipedia is reliable; Federal Court case law suggests it is not normally reliable evidence for the Board.
propositions.quote: For the same reason, I do not need to decide on whether Wikipedia is a reliable source; however, I note that the Federal Court case law suggests that it is not the sort of evidence the Board normally should rely on.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD breached Rule 22 by relying on Wikipedia but will not consider it in reassessment and will not set aside RPD decision.

propositions.text: Draws negative credibility finding based on Appellant's limited knowledge of HDP, considering limited education and some limited information given.
propositions.quote: I draw a negative credibility finding based on the Appellant's limited knowledge of the HDP in the circumstances. In making this finding, I have had regard to his limited education and to the fact that he was able to give some limited information about the HDP.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant not credible due to limited knowledge of the HDP, despite limited education and some information provided.

propositions.text: RPD found negative credibility due to failure to procure reasonably available supporting evidence in six categories.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a series of negative credibility findings based on the Appellant's failure to make reasonable attempts to procure supporting evidence that should have been reasonably available.

propositions.text: Lack of evidence showing financial support to HDP; no explanation for not seeking receipts later.
propositions.quote: It noted the lack of supporting evidence: 1) showing that he supported the HDP financially (the Appellant explained that he had not asked for a receipt but he gave no explanation as to why he had not sought receipts at a later point, i.e., while in Canada);

propositions.text: No family member evidence attesting to support; explanations rejected due to representation and family contact.
propositions.quote: 2) from his family members who could attest to his support for the HDP (the RPD rejected his explanations that he did not think about it or see the need, noting that he was well-represented and had regular contact with his family);

propositions.text: No evidence from other HDP members or volunteers confirming activities; no explanation for lack of efforts except letter submitted.
propositions.quote: 3) from other HDP members or volunteers to confirm his activities for the Party (when asked why he had not made efforts, he provided no explanation, other than noting that he had submitted a letter from the HDP);

propositions.text: No evidence supporting claim of paying extortion money multiple times, e.g. bank records.
propositions.quote: 4) to support his claim that he had paid extortion money ten to twelve times, e.g. bank records;

propositions.text: No evidence showing closure or ownership of XXXX XXXX.
propositions.quote: 5) to show that the XXXX XXXX was closed or that he and his family owned a XXXX XXXX;

propositions.text: No evidence supporting 2019 raid or two-day detention claims.
propositions.quote: 6) to support the XXXX 2019 raid on his home or his two-day detention.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant lacked credibility due to failure to provide reasonably available supporting evidence in six specific areas.

propositions.text: Appellant argues inability to provide receipts because he did not ask for them.
propositions.quote: First, the Appellant argues that he was unable to provide receipts of his donations to the HDP because he did not ask for them.

propositions.text: Argues letter from HDP is arguably best possible evidence; no need for more supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: Second, he argues that he had no reason to adduce more supporting evidence to show his involvement with the HDP because his letter from the HDP was arguably the "best possible evidence."

propositions.text: Relies on letters from father and brother as new evidence at appeal.
propositions.quote: Finally, he relies on the letters from his father and brother as new evidence at appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues he could not provide receipts, that the HDP letter is best evidence, and relies on new family letters at appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant does not contest RPD findings on lack of evidence for items 4-6; court agrees with RPD reasoning.
propositions.quote: Because the Appellant does not contest the RPD's findings regarding the lack of documents discussed at items 4)-6) above, I will not address these findings in this decision. I note, however, that I have considered the RPD's reasoning and agree with it.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appellant does not contest RPD's findings on some evidence gaps and agrees with RPD's reasoning.

propositions.text: Negative credibility finding means loss of Maldonado presumption of truthfulness.
propositions.quote: My negative credibility finding based on the Appellant's limited knowledge of the HDP means that he has lost the benefit of the Maldonado presumption that his sworn evidence is truthful.

propositions.text: No need to consider interplay between burden of proof and Maldonado presumption.
propositions.quote: Consequently, I need not consider the interplay between his obligation to prove his claim, as per RPD Rule 11, and the Maldonado presumption.

propositions.text: Federal Court says adverse credibility findings on lack of corroboration require valid reason to doubt or rejection of explanation for missing evidence.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court recognized that it is an error to make an adverse credibility finding on the basis of the absence of corroborative evidence unless 1) there is a valid reason to doubt the claimant's credibility or 2) the decision-maker does not accept the claimant's explanation for failing to produce such evidence when it would be reasonably expected to be available.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant lost the Maldonado presumption and cites Federal Court law on adverse credibility findings based on missing corroboration.

propositions.text: Accepts appellant's explanation for not asking for receipts is reasonable but notes failure to seek receipts after arrival in Canada is concerning.
propositions.quote: First, I accept that the Appellant's explanation that he did not ask for receipts is reasonable as far as it goes.

propositions.text: RPD's concern was appellant made no efforts to obtain receipts after coming to Canada and gave no reasonable explanation.
propositions.quote: However, the RPD's concern was focussed on the fact that the Appellant made no efforts to obtain receipts showing his donations to the party after the fact-i.e. after he came to Canada and pursued a refugee claim-and provided no reasonable explanation why.

propositions.text: Donation receipts are available per country condition evidence; failure to explain failure to obtain them warrants negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: Given that donation receipts are available according to the country condition evidence, I find that his failure to explain why he opted not to obtain them warrants a negative credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts the appellant's initial explanation but finds failure to seek receipts after arrival in Canada justifies negative credibility finding.

propositions.text: Appellant's claim that HDP letter is more probative than family or volunteer letters might be true if letter was personalized and detailed, but it is not.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's claim that a letter from the HDP is more probative than a letter from his family members or his fellow HDP volunteers might be true if the letter directly corresponded with his evidence, was personalized in nature, and was more detailed.

propositions.text: Even if HDP letter is best evidence, Board's expectation for more supporting evidence is not incorrect, especially for core claim issues.
propositions.quote: Moreover, even if a letter from the Party is highly probative or the "best possible evidence" of the Appellant's links to the HDP, it does not necessarily follow that the Board's expectation that there would be more supporting evidence was incorrect.

propositions.text: It is usual for RPD to expect more than one item of objective proof on a core claim issue like political affiliation.
propositions.quote: It is certainly not unusual for the RPD to expect, and for a claimant to provide, more than a single item of objective proof on an issue, in particular one that is at the very heart of a claim-in this case, a connection to the HDP that the Appellant claims has led to his detention and may in the future lead to persecution or other harm.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the HDP letter lacks personalization and detail, and the Board's expectation for more evidence on core claim issues is reasonable.

propositions.text: Letters from appellant's brother and father found inadmissible and cannot be considered.
propositions.quote: Finally, I note that I have found the letters from the Appellant's brother and father inadmissible above. I cannot, of course, consider inadmissible evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the family letters inadmissible and will not consider them.

propositions.text: Given nature of HDP letter and importance of proving claim, RPD was correct to expect more supporting evidence from represented claimant.
propositions.quote: In view of the nature of the letter that the Appellant provided and the importance of proving his claim, including that he was affiliated with the HDP, I agree that the RPD was correct to expect there be more supporting evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant, especially if represented, must provide sufficient evidence to prove claim.
propositions.quote: As discussed above in my assessment of the new evidence the Appellant proposed at appeal, it falls to a claimant-in particular one who is represented but experienced counsel-to provide sufficient evidence to prove their claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the RPD was correct to expect more evidence from the represented appellant to prove his claim.

propositions.text: RPD gave little weight to 2020 HDP letter as it was silent on long-standing support and important functions claimed by appellant.
propositions.quote: The RPD placed little weight on the XXXX XXXX, 2020 supporting letter from the HDP-the sole supporting document linking him to the HDP-noting that it was silent regarding his claim to have been a long-standing HDP supporter with who undertook certain important functions such as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Letter's description of appellant's contributions did not match his evidence; letter mentioned congresses and exhibitions not in his evidence.
propositions.quote: It noted that the description of the Appellant's contributions in the letter-that he had worked in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX-did not jibe with his evidence, i.e., that that he engaged in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, provided financial donations, and worked at a XXXX XXXX. It noted further that he made no mention in his evidence of his having participated in congresses or exhibitions.

propositions.text: Letter appeared to be a template with no personal details.
propositions.quote: The RPD also noted that the letter appeared to be a template and had no personal details.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the HDP letter lacked detail, did not match appellant's evidence, and appeared templated.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred by dismissing letter for what it lacks rather than what it says.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that the HDP letter warranted little weight because i) it erred by dismissing supporting evidence because of what it does not say, rather than considering it for what it does say;

propositions.text: Argues template letter can still be largely accurate and apply to appellant.
propositions.quote: ii) even if it is a template, it does not mean that it is not largely accurate or that it does not largely apply to the Appellant;

propositions.text: Claims RPD was being microscopic; 'congresses' and 'exhibitions' could include meetings or volunteering.
propositions.quote: iii) it was being microscopic-after all, "congresses" and "exhibition" are broad enough that they could include attending meetings at the HDP office or volunteering at an XXXX XXXX;

propositions.text: Argues letter suffices to prove party membership, which is all needed for claim success.
propositions.quote: iv) the letter was sufficient to prove to the RPD's satisfaction that he was a member of the Party-which, as he argues below, is all that is necessary for his claim to succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred by dismissing the HDP letter for omissions, that template letters can be accurate, and that the letter suffices to prove membership.

propositions.text: RPD did not reject letter for omissions but found it less probative due to lack of personalization and mismatch with appellant's evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD did not reject the letter because of what it did not say. Instead, it found that it warranted less weight as evidence to support the Appellant's claim that he had a strong affiliation with the HDP, given that it was not personalized and its description of the work undertaken by the Appellant did not fully jibe with the Appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: Adeleye case says discounting evidence for what it does not say does not detract from need for sufficient evidence to ground well-founded fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: As Mr. Justice Grammond held in Adeleye, the prohibition on discounting evidence for what it does not say-i.e. disbelieving one witness's evidence simply because another witness corroborated only part of that evidence and remained silent as to another part-"does not detract from the general requirement that there be sufficient evidence to ground a finding of a well-founded fear of persecution."

propositions.text: Template letter is less probative than personalized letter that matches claimant's story.
propositions.quote: Its point was that a letter, such as this one, which has little or no personalized detail about a member of a political party, is less probative than a letter that described the specific contribution of the claimant in a personalized way-and did so in a way that jibed with the story told by the claimant.

propositions.text: Letter does not correspond with appellant's evidence: omits claimed contributions and includes unmentioned congresses and exhibitions.
propositions.quote: In this case, the letter from the HDP does not correspond with the Appellant's evidence in two ways: first, it fails to include contributions that the Appellant claims to have made... and second, it includes contributions that the Appellant does not mention in his evidence (attendance at congresses and exhibitions).

propositions.text: Close examination of sole supporting evidence is not microscopic; contributions and repercussions are core to claim.
propositions.quote: I can see no basis upon which a close examination of the only evidence supporting the Appellant's link to the HDP, in order to determine if it supports his claims, may be characterized as microscopic.

propositions.text: Letter's reference to congresses or exhibitions cannot be presumed to include visits or volunteering at HDP headquarters.
propositions.quote: I disagree that the letter's reference to attendance at "congresses" or "exhibitions" may be read to include the Appellant's claim to have visited at the HDP headquarters and to have volunteered at XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD reasonably gave less weight to the templated HDP letter due to lack of personalization and mismatch with appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: HDP letter has probative value but less due to general nature, lack of membership duration, and mismatched activities.
propositions.quote: I accept the letter from the HDP has probative value. Having said that, the letter is of less value that it would otherwise be because it is general in nature, it does not elaborate on the length of time he has been a member of or associated with the Party, and some of the activities it states that the Appellant engaged in he did not mention in his evidence and other activities he claims to have engaged in are not mentioned in the letter.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts the HDP letter has some probative value but is weakened by its generality and inconsistencies with appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: Weighing credibility concerns and limited evidence, court finds appellant lacks credibility and was not HDP member or persecuted.
propositions.quote: When I weigh the above credibility concerns alongside the Appellant's extraordinarily limited supporting evidence...I find that he is lacking in credibility. I find that the letter from the HDP does not outweigh my credibility concerns. As such, I find that the Appellant was not a member of the HDP, did not assist the Party, was not pursued by the Turkish authorities based on his actual or perceived political opinion, was not extorted by the Turkish authorities, and was not detained or threatened with torture.

propositions.text: Consequently, appellant does not face serious possibility of persecution or likelihood of harm under subsection 97(1).
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find that he does not face a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of his political affiliation (or perceived political affiliation); nor does he face a likelihood of harm as per subsection 97(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant not credible, not an HDP member, not persecuted, and not at risk of persecution or harm under subsection 97(1).

propositions.text: Appellant lost Maldonado presumption and has not met burden to prove serious possibility of persecution or likelihood of harm.
propositions.quote: In addition, having regard to the limited evidence that has been provided and the Appellant's loss of the Maldonado presumption, I find that he has not met his burden of proving that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of his past political affiliation (or perceived political affiliation); nor has he shown that he faces a likelihood of harm as per subsection 97(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant failed to prove serious possibility of persecution or likelihood of harm after losing the Maldonado presumption.

propositions.text: Appellant argues country evidence shows active HDP supporters face persecution risk if openly political and future ban could cause persecution risk.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues i) that even if I doubt his specific allegations, the country condition evidence shows that active HDP supporters or members are at risk of persecution if they voice their political opinion openly; and ii) that there is no guarantee that the Turkish authorities will not ban the HDP altogether and, if it does so, there is no guarantee that he will not be at risk of persecution solely on the basis that he was a member of the Party.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues country evidence shows HDP supporters face persecution risk and future party ban could cause persecution risk.

propositions.text: Court accepts appellant is Kurdish but finds he was not HDP member or assistant, so no need to consider treatment of HDP members.
propositions.quote: While I accept that he has proven that he is Kurdish, as noted above, I have found that he was not a member of the HDP and that he did not assist the Party. Consequently, I need not consider how a person who was an HDP member or supporter would be treated-whether that person is Kurdish or not.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts the appellant is Kurdish but finds he was not an HDP member or assistant, so does not consider treatment of HDP members.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed; RPD decision confirmed under paragraph 111(1)(a) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the decision of the RPD. The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision under IRPA paragraph 111(1)(a).
